title: Court documents reveal details of Winnipeg man's alleged Bishnoi gang extortion
summary: A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter…

image.caption: Arshdeep Brar, 36, is accused in a Winnipeg extortion case allegedly involving the India-based Bishnoi gang. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter to the man's home threatening his family.
Letter sent to victim this year says 'mistakes will not be forgiven'

A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone outside a Sobeys in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter in Hindi to the man's home threatening his family and telling him to leave $150,000 in cash at a site along a highway.

Details about how that case allegedly unfolded earlier this year were revealed in court documents — including an arrest report, affidavit and police narrative — filed in a criminal property forfeiture case against Arshdeep Brar, 36, who was eventually charged for his alleged involvement.
The documents, filed in July, also include a photo of the alleged threat letter and an English translation of its contents.
"Remember I have all the information of your house, your wife, kids and even your brother in India," it said, warning the victim not to contact police or "be clever with me."
"Mistakes will not be forgiven."

The unnamed victim, described only as a person in Winnipeg of South Asian descent, told police he got the first phone call in February from someone who introduced himself as Pardeep Jayani from the international Bishnoi gang, the documents allege. That call was made from outside the Sobeys on Dakota Street.

The criminal organization primarily operates out of India and is run by Lawrence Bishnoi, who has been in a prison in that country since 2015. The gang, which Canada designated a terrorist group in 2025, targets South Asian diaspora communities and is involved with criminal activities such as extortion, contract killings, arson, intimidation, and drug and firearm trafficking.
A photo of the letter allegedly sent to the victim was included in court documents. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)
Police announced last week that one of the group's top lieutenants, Satinderjeet Singh — also known as Goldy Brar — is wanted alongside another man in a 2023 murder in Winnipeg.
In the recent Winnipeg extortion case, court documents said when the victim got the call asking for money, he panicked "and didn't know what to say or do after he heard [the name] Bishnoi."

blocks.text: "[Redacted] has no issues with anyone. [Redacted] found it odd that the demand was not made via WhatsApp call as that's the common way Bishnoi gang operates," the documents said.
"[Redacted] knows another [redacted] in Winnipeg who went through the same circumstances. [Redacted] doesn't know how he managed to settle the deal."
The court documents also included this version of the letter, which has English translations of each paragraph. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)
Brar is accused of calling the victim twice, including a second time from a payphone at Watt Street and Jamison Avenue, in Winnipeg's Elmwood area.
During the phone calls, the victim said the person on the other end told him he would "notify his boss, Aarzoo Bishnoi" and that the victim "would have to face the consequences."

The victim said he also told the person at one point that he "doesn't have that much money and that he is not into illegal things." He said the person replied that he "doesn't care how he arranges the money, but he must do it," the documents allege.

The letter Brar allegedly sent the victim, demanding cash be left in a bag by a yellow gate near a highway rest area outside Portage la Prairie, Man., said "it's not hard to find people to do shootings," for only $5,000 or $6,000.
"If any of my boys get caught, that will be your responsibility," the translated letter said.
Accused 'directed' by gang

Brar ended up being arrested and charged after picking up a package of money police had prepared and delivered to the specified drop-off location, the documents allege. The director of the province's criminal property forfeiture branch is now seeking to seize the truck it says was involved in the crime.
The court documents state Brar and the victim were acquaintances and that both "were working [redacted] in Winnipeg at the time of the incident."
Brar told police he sent the letter to the victim demanding $150,000, but said he "took this action because he was directed to do so by a member of the Bishnoi Gang," the documents allege.

blocks.text: In a statement of defence filed by Brar and his wife — whose name the truck is registered in — he denied phoning the victim, being a member of the Bishnoi group or writing the letter.

"In the alternative … Brar pleads that any involvement he had in the transmission or delivery of a letter occurred under compulsion, threat, or coercion from another person who identified themselves as a member of the Bishnoi Gang," the filing said.

Brar's wife said there were no material facts that she participated in or knew about any unlawful activity, and the forfeiture of her interest in the truck would be unjust. The couple's filing seeks to dismiss the forfeiture claim on the vehicle.
Winnipeg case rare: expert

Wade Deisman, an associate professor in the University of the Fraser Valley's criminology school in British Columbia, said because of the pervasive sense of fear that the Bishnoi gang has created in Indian diaspora communities, many people targeted for extortion don't go to police.
That makes the Winnipeg case rare because the person sought help, and because police were able to charge someone, he said.

Deisman also said the suggestion in the case that it was unusual the alleged perpetrator used phone calls and letters instead of WhatsApp "raises the spectre" of whether there are copycat operations happening that aren't actually affiliated with the Bishnoi gang.
But once that deep fear develops in a community, "it becomes kind of immaterial" who's behind a threat like that, said Deisman, who is researching some of the impacts of the Bishnoi gang.

blocks.text: "Sometimes a criminal organization will go after people who kind of get on their coattails," he said. "Sometimes they'll recruit them. Sometimes they'll punish them. Sometimes they won't do anything because it still builds their name and still builds their reputation."
The charges against Brar have not been proven in court, and he is considered innocent unless proven guilty.
